name: Grey cast iron: Victorian architectural castings
summary: Grey (flake-graphite) cast iron: remelted pig iron with about 4 % carbon, poured into green-sand moulds, strong in compression and brittle in tension. In Albion it makes the clustered shafts that rise from the stone capitals (6.2 to 9.7 m) on bolted shoes, the ridges, ventilators, rainwater heads and downpipes; it is always seen painted.

formation.how: Iron ore is smelted in a blast furnace to pig iron, which carries 4 to 4.5 % carbon. The founder remelts the pig (in a cupola) and pours it at about 1300 degC into a mould of green sand rammed round a wooden pattern made about one per cent oversize, because the iron shrinks as it cools. As it freezes, most of the carbon comes out of solution as flakes of graphite, randomly oriented, which give a fresh fracture its grey, crystalline look and act as voids with sharp corners: the iron is very strong in compression, but in tension it cracks and fails abruptly. The skin that freezes against the sand is hard and resists corrosion better than a machined face.

optics.note: Victorian iron is never seen bare in Albion: it is always under its paint (painted.iron), whose optics are a dielectric coat. For a cut or worn-through edge, the bare metal's constants are those of iron, already recorded (Johnson and Christy 1974) in the steel record; a grey cast iron's graphite flakes and a wrought iron's slag stringers lower and darken a bare face but were not measured here.

spectral.text: Iron n,k (0.381-0.756 um) and the derived F0 and F82 triples are in the steel record; they are not copied here.
spectral.source: MuseeVision/Data/Matter/Substances/steel.json (optics.spectral: P. B. Johnson and R. W. Christy 1974, Fe; optics.f0)

acoustic.note: The iron members are slender and overhead; they are not an absorbing surface of the court. What the design asks of them is sound, not absorption: 'Rain runs down the glass and drums on the ribs' (Albion's Outside board), which is Sound's to model.

design.text: Rain runs down the glass and drums on the ribs; the court goes a stop darker and the band dims.

castings.text: Castings are made one pattern at a time: a shaft, a shoe or a rainwater head is a single pour, so there is no stock length; joints are bolted flanges and spigots, not welds.

oxford.text: Oxford University Museum of Natural History (Woodward, with Francis Skidmore of Coventry for the iron): clusters of iron columns and girders; the capitals of the iron clusters carry wrought-iron flowers and foliage; sixteen botanical spandrels in the central aisle. The roof's painted decoration was altered during building and repainted in April 1864 by G. Thicke and J. Randall (an inscription found in 2013).
oxford.source: Oxford University Museum of Natural History, 'Design and decoration: Central Court Roof', https://oum-ox.shorthandstories.com/oumnh-design-and-decoration/central-court-roof/

asBuilt.text: The as-built court (D-017) painted all its iron one dark slate grey, satin, as a non-metal: the values are the paint's, recorded in painted.iron.

photograph: Look for the paint, not the metal: many coats softening the arrises of the castings, runs and sags in the hollows of the cluster.
Cast details: parting lines where the mould halves met, draft on the faces, generous fillets, bolt heads and nuts at every flange, no welds anywhere.
Where the paint has failed (at shoes, bolt heads and anywhere water lies), rust bleeds down from the joint.

familyDeclaration.text: D-014 admits the families stone, white, bronze, oak, accent, glass, water and living; an accent names the core family it ties back to. Albion's iron exists to carry the glass of the vaults and screens (the stone stops at the capitals; above 6.2 m everything is iron and glass), as the Rotunda's steel lattice does, so it is declared an accent of the glass family, the same reading the metal group made for steel. The Architect may overturn it.

unverified.reason: Grey iron's density is commonly quoted near 7.1-7.2 g/cm3, but only weak web sources (and one listing 7.5 g/cm3) were read; no handbook value was confirmed.
Commonly quoted near 10-11 x 10^-6 /K for grey iron; no primary source was read.

A case-study paper on failed historic cast-iron columns (Infrastructures 5(9) 71, MDPI 2020) is reported by a search summary to give C 3.2-3.3, Si 0.9-1.1, P 0.2-0.3, Mn 1.1-1.7, S 0.05-0.07 wt% for later-19th-century iron; the paper could not be read (HTTP 403).
Bracketing Victorian structural grey iron by ASTM A48 Classes 20-30 is this record's reading of Bussell's qualitative account; historic test data (Bussell's SCI appraisal guide) were not read.
